It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
Matteo is a 21-year-old married man who works in social ministry, and when he speaks about the months he spent as a relief worker in a war zone, he does so in a flat, disbelieving way, as if he is describing something that happened to somebody else. The event he returns to most often took place during a chaotic aid distribution outside a damaged building, when shouting in Arabic suddenly rose around him and the crowd surged. He remembers men moving quickly in all directions, arms lifting, bodies pushing, voices turning sharp and urgent. In the confusion he became certain that he and the others with him were about to be killed. Even now, what unnerves him is not only the danger he was in, but how unreal the memory feels: it is so extreme that he still struggles to accept that it really happened to him.

After he came home to the United States and tried to return to ordinary life with his wife, Matteo found that very specific moments pierced that sense of distance and made the scene crash back in. If someone nearby was shouting in Arabic, or if conversation turned to the military, or if someone asked him directly about his relief work, he did not simply remember the event. The memory arrived with the same terror he had felt there, and it felt present rather than over, as though the room around him had briefly been replaced by the crowd and noise of that day. Because recalling it in words could set this off, even talking about the event itself became one of the things that could trigger it.

Those moments changed how he moved through daily life. In his ministry job, where he meets unfamiliar people and often hears emotionally intense conversations, he has become tense around strangers approaching him in perfectly ordinary situations. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. When a raised voice or military topic catches him off balance, he scans the room before he has fully realized he is doing it, his body acting as if danger is close. At night he wakes and checks whether he is safe, listening to the apartment and orienting himself before he can settle again. The more on edge he feels, the more easily he notices the very things that set him off—an abrupt gesture, a certain language, any drift toward discussing conflict—so that his days have begun to feel organized around anticipating impact. On the nights when that sense of danger is strongest, the aid distribution scene comes back more readily, as if staying braced for attack keeps the memory close at hand and easier for his mind to slip into.

He has tried to manage this in ways that make sense to him in the moment. After a difficult day, especially if something at work has stirred the memory, he stays up until very late because sleep feels like lowering his guard. In the quiet hours he goes over the event repeatedly, thinking about how it could have been prevented, replaying decisions and alternatives as if he might finally find the point where catastrophe became avoidable. He also pulls back from situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful. Instead of settling the experience, these late-night reviews make it more vivid, and the more he tries to hold himself away from anything that might stir him, the less digested the memory feels, returning with the same force the next time it is touched. Part of him feels these lighter moments are unsafe, too exposed, too likely to be interrupted by the memory; another part seems unwilling to let himself enjoy anything while that day remains unresolved in his mind.

These habits have gradually tightened the problem. The late nights leave him worn down and brittle, and in that exhausted state the memory comes back even more forcefully, with less distance and more of the original terror. Rumination does not give him an answer; it keeps the event emotionally alive, as if he is standing inside it trying once again to change the outcome. Avoiding positive moments narrows his life until there is less that feels distinct from the trauma, fewer experiences that might anchor him in the present. His wife has noticed that he is harder to reach and that even casual evenings together can abruptly close down if a news segment mentions the military or a question about his overseas work slips into conversation.

Lately the cycle has become harder for Matteo to hide. In one recent ministry meeting, a visitor’s loud Arabic shouting in the hallway made him freeze and feel the terror surge up so completely that for a moment he was no longer sure he was in the church office at all. Afterward he stayed up most of the night, checking locks, replaying the scene overseas, and thinking again about what should have been done differently. He has come for help because he is frightened by how quickly ordinary life disappears when he is triggered, and by how suspicious and alert he has become around people he knows are not threatening. More than anything, he wants to believe that the event is truly over, and fears that if this continues, he will remain trapped in a world where it keeps happening now.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state that Matteo’s sense of threat itself leads to or intensifies the trauma memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state that Matteo’s maladaptive strategies cause or increase the trauma memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
